brief.topic: Korean Hangul alphabet and high-frequency sight words
brief.outcome: An English-speaking learner can recognize core Hangul symbols and understand common Korean words and phrases on sight.
brief.audience: English-speaking Korean language learner at beginner level
brief.direction: English to Korean where requested; otherwise prompt-to-answer recall.
brief.language: English explanations with Korean examples where relevant
assumptions: Cards are study prompts, not professional advice.
Romanization is a pronunciation aid, not a replacement for Hangul.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — Korean language resources
sources.notes: Official Korean language institution used for Hangul terminology and orthographic conventions.

sources.title: Korean-English Learners' Dictionary
sources.notes: National Institute of Korean Language learner dictionary used for English glosses and usage notes.

claims.text: What consonant is **ㄱ**, and what is its usual sound guide? — ㄱ is *기역* (giyeok). It is roughly **g** at the beginning of a syllable and **k** at the end; exact pronunciation depends on position and surrounding sounds.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㄱ is *기역* (giyeok). It is roughly **g** at the beginning of a syllable and **k** at the end; exact pronunciation depends on position and surrounding sounds.

claims.text: What consonant is **ㄴ**, and what sound does it represent? — ㄴ is *니은* (nieun) and represents an **n** sound.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㄴ is *니은* (nieun) and represents an **n** sound.

claims.text: What consonant is **ㄷ**, and what is its usual sound guide? — ㄷ is *디귿* (digeut). It is roughly **d** initially and **t** finally.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㄷ is *디귿* (digeut). It is roughly **d** initially and **t** finally.

claims.text: What consonant is **ㄹ**, and why is its romanization context-dependent? — ㄹ is *리을* (rieul). It is commonly realized between an **r-like** sound in some onset positions and an **l-like** sound in coda or doubled contexts; English romanization is only an approximation.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㄹ is *리을* (rieul). It is commonly realized between an **r-like** sound in some onset positions and an **l-like** sound in coda or doubled contexts; English romanization is only an approximation.

claims.text: What consonant is **ㅁ**, and what sound does it represent? — ㅁ is *미음* (mieum) and represents **m**.
What consonant is **ㅂ**, and what is its usual sound guide? — ㅂ is *비읍* (bieup). It is roughly **b** initially and **p** finally.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅂ is *비읍* (bieup). It is roughly **b** initially and **p** finally.

claims.text: What consonant is **ㅅ**, and what sound does it usually represent? — ㅅ is *시옷* (siot) and is usually **s**, with context-dependent pronunciation before certain vowels.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅅ is *시옷* (siot) and is usually **s**, with context-dependent pronunciation before certain vowels.

claims.text: What are the two main roles of **ㅇ**? — At the beginning of a syllable block, ㅇ is silent; at the end, it represents **ng** as in English *sing*.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: At the beginning of a syllable block, ㅇ is silent; at the end, it represents **ng** as in English *sing*.

claims.text: What consonant is **ㅈ**, and what is its sound guide? — ㅈ is *지읒* (jieut) and is roughly **j** or a soft affricate sound.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅈ is *지읒* (jieut) and is roughly **j** or a soft affricate sound.

claims.text: What consonant is **ㅊ**, and how does it differ from ㅈ? — ㅊ is *치읓* (chieut) and is an aspirated **ch** sound; ㅈ is the less-aspirated counterpart.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅊ is *치읓* (chieut) and is an aspirated **ch** sound; ㅈ is the less-aspirated counterpart.

claims.text: What consonant is **ㅋ**, and what sound does it represent? — ㅋ is *키읔* (kieuk) and is an aspirated **k** sound.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅋ is *키읔* (kieuk) and is an aspirated **k** sound.

claims.text: What consonant is **ㅌ**, and what sound does it represent? — ㅌ is *티읕* (tieut) and is an aspirated **t** sound.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅌ is *티읕* (tieut) and is an aspirated **t** sound.

claims.text: What consonant is **ㅍ**, and what sound does it represent? — ㅍ is *피읖* (pieup) and is an aspirated **p** sound.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅍ is *피읖* (pieup) and is an aspirated **p** sound.

claims.text: What consonant is **ㅎ**, and what sound does it represent? — ㅎ is *히읗* (hieut) and is an **h** sound, with predictable effects on neighboring consonants.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅎ is *히읗* (hieut) and is an **h** sound, with predictable effects on neighboring consonants.

claims.text: What vowel is **ㅏ**, and what sound guide is commonly used? — ㅏ is *아* and is commonly represented as **a**, similar to the vowel in *father* for many learners.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅏ is *아* and is commonly represented as **a**, similar to the vowel in *father* for many learners.

claims.text: What vowel is **ㅑ**, and what sound guide is commonly used? — ㅑ is *야* and is commonly represented as **ya**.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅑ is *야* and is commonly represented as **ya**.

claims.text: What vowel is **ㅓ**, and why is **eo** only an approximation? — ㅓ is *어*. Revised Romanization writes it **eo**; English has no exact equivalent, so learners should use Korean audio rather than treating the spelling as two sounds.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅓ is *어*. Revised Romanization writes it **eo**; English has no exact equivalent, so learners should use Korean audio rather than treating the spelling as two sounds.

claims.text: What vowel is **ㅕ**, and what sound guide is commonly used? — ㅕ is *여* and is commonly represented as **yeo**.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅕ is *여* and is commonly represented as **yeo**.

claims.text: What vowel is **ㅗ**, and what sound guide is commonly used? — ㅗ is *오* and is commonly represented as **o**.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅗ is *오* and is commonly represented as **o**.

claims.text: What vowel is **ㅛ**, and what sound guide is commonly used? — ㅛ is *요* and is commonly represented as **yo**.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅛ is *요* and is commonly represented as **yo**.

claims.text: What vowel is **ㅜ**, and what sound guide is commonly used? — ㅜ is *우* and is commonly represented as **u**, roughly like the vowel in *boot* for many learners.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅜ is *우* and is commonly represented as **u**, roughly like the vowel in *boot* for many learners.

claims.text: What vowel is **ㅠ**, and what sound guide is commonly used? — ㅠ is *유* and is commonly represented as **yu**.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅠ is *유* and is commonly represented as **yu**.

claims.text: What vowel is **ㅡ**, and why is **eu** only a learner guide? — ㅡ is *으*. Revised Romanization writes it **eu**; it is a Korean vowel without a direct English equivalent.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅡ is *으*. Revised Romanization writes it **eu**; it is a Korean vowel without a direct English equivalent.

claims.text: What vowel is **ㅣ**, and what sound does it represent? — ㅣ is *이* and represents **i**, like the vowel in *machine* for many learners.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅣ is *이* and represents **i**, like the vowel in *machine* for many learners.

claims.text: What is the common sound guide for **ㅐ**? — ㅐ is *애* and is written **ae**; in modern Seoul Korean its pronunciation is often close to ㅔ for many speakers.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅐ is *애* and is written **ae**; in modern Seoul Korean its pronunciation is often close to ㅔ for many speakers.

claims.text: What is the common sound guide for **ㅔ**? — ㅔ is *에* and is written **e**; it is distinct in spelling even though many speakers pronounce it similarly to ㅐ.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅔ is *에* and is written **e**; it is distinct in spelling even though many speakers pronounce it similarly to ㅐ.

claims.text: How is **ㅘ** formed and pronounced? — ㅘ is a compound vowel written **wa**, formed from ㅗ plus ㅏ.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅘ is a compound vowel written **wa**, formed from ㅗ plus ㅏ.

claims.text: How is **ㅝ** formed and pronounced? — ㅝ is a compound vowel written **wo**, formed from ㅜ plus ㅓ.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅝ is a compound vowel written **wo**, formed from ㅜ plus ㅓ.

claims.text: How is **ㅚ** commonly romanized, and what pronunciation variation should learners know? — ㅚ is commonly romanized **oe**; modern pronunciation is often close to **we** in many contexts, so audio matters.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅚ is commonly romanized **oe**; modern pronunciation is often close to **we** in many contexts, so audio matters.

claims.text: What is the usual sound guide for **ㅟ**? — ㅟ is *위* and is commonly represented as **wi**.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: ㅟ is *위* and is commonly represented as **wi**.

claims.text: How are Hangul syllable blocks constructed? — A syllable block combines an initial consonant, a vowel, and optionally a final consonant. The letters are arranged into one visual block, not written as a horizontal alphabetic string.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: A syllable block combines an initial consonant, a vowel, and optionally a final consonant. The letters are arranged into one visual block, not written as a horizontal alphabetic string.

claims.text: How can you decompose **한** into its jamo? — **한** is ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ: initial ㅎ, vowel ㅏ, and final consonant ㄴ.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: **한** is ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ: initial ㅎ, vowel ㅏ, and final consonant ㄴ.

claims.text: What does **받침** (batchim) mean in Hangul reading? — 받침 is the final consonant position at the bottom of a syllable block. Its pronunciation follows Korean final-consonant rules and may change before the next syllable.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: 받침 is the final consonant position at the bottom of a syllable block. Its pronunciation follows Korean final-consonant rules and may change before the next syllable.

claims.text: What sound family do final ㄱ, ㅋ, and ㄲ commonly represent? — In final position, ㄱ, ㅋ, and ㄲ are commonly realized as the unreleased **[k̚]**-type sound; they are not pronounced like a fully released English k.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: In final position, ㄱ, ㅋ, and ㄲ are commonly realized as the unreleased **[k̚]**-type sound; they are not pronounced like a fully released English k.

claims.text: What sound does final **ㅇ** commonly represent? — Final ㅇ represents **ng**, as in the ending of English *sing*.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: Final ㅇ represents **ng**, as in the ending of English *sing*.

claims.text: What does a double consonant such as **ㄲ** indicate? — A doubled jamo such as ㄲ is a tense consonant, not simply a longer version of ㄱ. Tense consonants have different articulation and are best learned with audio.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: A doubled jamo such as ㄲ is a tense consonant, not simply a longer version of ㄱ. Tense consonants have different articulation and are best learned with audio.

cards.front: What does **안녕하세요** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: annyeonghaseyo (an-nyeong-ha-se-yo). Usage note: Standard polite greeting; use with people when a neutral polite register is appropriate.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **안녕** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: annyeong (an-nyeong). Usage note: Informal greeting and farewell used with close friends or people of similar age when appropriate.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **감사합니다** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: gamsahamnida (gam-sa-ham-ni-da). Usage note: Formal or highly polite expression of thanks.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **고마워요** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: gomawoyo (go-ma-wo-yo). Usage note: Polite but less formal than 감사합니다; common in friendly polite speech.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **네** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: ne (neh). Usage note: Often used to agree or acknowledge; context can make it closer to “okay” or “I hear you.”
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **아니요** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: aniyo (a-ni-yo). Usage note: Polite negative response.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **죄송합니다** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: joesonghamnida (joe-song-ham-ni-da). Usage note: Formal/polite apology; stronger and more formal than 미안해요.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **미안해요** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: mianhaeyo (mi-an-hae-yo). Usage note: Polite apology in a friendlier register.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **괜찮아요** mean in common Korean?
cards.back: it is okay / I am fine
cards.extra: Pronunciation: gwaenchanayo (gwen-cha-na-yo). Usage note: Can reassure someone, say that something is acceptable, or answer a “how are you?”-type question depending on context.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **주세요** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: juseyo (ju-se-yo). Usage note: Polite request form, often following a noun: 물 주세요 = Please give me water.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **뭐** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: mwo (mwuh). Usage note: Conversational form of 무엇; used in questions such as 뭐예요? = What is it?
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **어디** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: eodi (uh-di). Usage note: Question word for location.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **누구** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: nugu (nu-gu). Usage note: Question word for a person.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **왜** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: wae (weh). Usage note: Question word for a reason.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **언제** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: eonje (un-je). Usage note: Question word for time.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **어떻게** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: eotteoke (uh-tuh-ke). Usage note: Question word for manner or method.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **이거** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: igeo (ee-guh). Usage note: Demonstrative noun meaning “this” in a conversational form.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **그거** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: geugeo (guh-guh). Usage note: Demonstrative noun meaning “that” near the listener or previously mentioned.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **저거** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: jeogeo (juh-guh). Usage note: Demonstrative noun for something away from both speaker and listener.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **여기** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: yeogi (yuh-gi). Usage note: Location near the speaker.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **거기** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: geogi (guh-gi). Usage note: Location near the listener or a previously mentioned place.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **저기** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: jeogi (juh-gi). Usage note: A location away from both speaker and listener; also used to get attention politely.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **오늘** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: oneul (oh-neul). Usage note: The current day.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **내일** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: naeil (neh-eel). Usage note: The day after today.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **어제** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: eoje (uh-je). Usage note: The day before today.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **지금** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: jigeum (ji-geum). Usage note: The current time or moment.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **사람** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: saram (sa-ram). Usage note: A person; the plural meaning can be understood from context.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **친구** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: chingu (chin-gu). Usage note: A friend; Korean does not require an article in the same way English does.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **집** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: jip (jeep). Usage note: Home or a house, depending on context.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **학교** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: hakgyo (hak-gyo). Usage note: School as a place or institution.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **물** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: mul (mool). Usage note: Water; often used in requests such as 물 주세요.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **밥** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: bap (bap). Usage note: Cooked rice and, by extension, a meal; context determines the best English gloss.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **화장실** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: hwajangsil (hwa-jang-shil). Usage note: Common word for a restroom or bathroom.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **이름** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: ireum (ee-reum). Usage note: A name; 이름이 뭐예요? = What is your name?
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **한국** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: Hanguk (han-guk). Usage note: The Korean name for Korea; context may specify South Korea or the Korean peninsula.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **영어** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: yeongeo (yung-uh). Usage note: The English language.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **좋아요** mean in common Korean?
cards.back: it is good / I like it
cards.extra: Pronunciation: joayo (jo-a-yo). Usage note: Polite present form of 좋다; common for approval or “I like it.”
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **싫어요** mean in common Korean?
cards.back: I dislike it / I do not like it
cards.extra: Pronunciation: silheoyo (sil-huh-yo). Usage note: Polite present form used to express dislike.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **있어요** mean in common Korean?
cards.back: there is / I have / it exists
cards.extra: Pronunciation: isseoyo (iss-uh-yo). Usage note: Polite form of 있다; meaning depends on context and location/possession.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **없어요** mean in common Korean?
cards.back: there is not / I do not have
cards.extra: Pronunciation: eopseoyo (uhp-suh-yo). Usage note: Polite form of 없다; indicates absence or non-possession.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **가요** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: gayo (ga-yo). Usage note: Polite present form of 가다.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **와요** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: wayo (wa-yo). Usage note: Polite present form of 오다.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **먹어요** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: meogeoyo (muh-guh-yo). Usage note: Polite present form of 먹다.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **마셔요** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: masyeoyo (ma-shuh-yo). Usage note: Polite present form of 마시다.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.

cards.front: What does **봐요** mean in common Korean?
cards.extra: Pronunciation: bwayo (bwa-yo). Usage note: Polite present form of 보다; translation depends on context.
cards.typeRationale: Basic recall is direct and unambiguous for this learning point.
